text: Your heart has four tiny doors that open and close about one hundred thousand times a day. If just one of them gets stiff, or starts to leak, the whole heart has to work harder. Let's see how heart valves can fail.
The four valves are the tricuspid, the pulmonary, the mitral, and the aortic valve. Each one is a one way door. It opens to let blood through, then snaps shut so blood can't flow backward.

A valve can go wrong in two main ways. It can become narrow and stiff, so it doesn't open fully. This is called stenosis. Or it can become leaky, so it doesn't close tightly. This is called regurgitation.

In stenosis, the heart must push blood through a tiny opening. Think of squeezing water through a pinched hose. Over time, the heart muscle thickens and gets tired. Aortic stenosis is common in older adults.
In regurgitation, some blood leaks backward with every beat. So the heart pumps the same blood again and again. To cope, the chamber stretches and gets bigger, and over time it can weaken.

What damages valves? Wear and calcium build up with age, rheumatic fever after an untreated strep throat, a valve someone is born with, an infection of the valve called endocarditis, and damage from a heart attack.

A faulty valve often makes an extra whooshing sound, called a heart murmur, that a doctor can hear with a stethoscope. The key test is an ultrasound of the heart, called an echocardiogram, which shows the valve moving.
Many people have no symptoms for years. Later there may be breathlessness, tiredness, chest pain, dizziness or fainting, and swollen ankles. Sudden chest pain or fainting needs urgent medical help.

Mild problems are often just checked regularly. Medicines can ease symptoms. When a valve is badly damaged, it can be repaired or replaced, by open heart surgery or through a thin tube in a blood vessel. And treating strep throat early helps prevent rheumatic heart disease.

So remember three things. Valves are one way doors. Stenosis means stiff and narrow, regurgitation means leaky. And an echocardiogram finds the problem. That completes the heart. Next, we'll move to the lungs and see how breathing works.
